newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada-U.S. border reopens after blizzard claims one life.
newsitem.headline: Canada-U.S. border reopens after blizzard claims one life.

text.p: The Canada-U.S. border opened and flights resumed Monday after a blizzard dumped 10 inches of snow here Sunday and claimed the life of at least one man.
"We've got one lane open and cars and trucks are crossing the border now," Canada Customs supervisor Denis Boyda said in a phone interview from the Emerson, Man., border crossing.

U.S. I-29 in North Dakota and I-75 in Minnesota were closed at 1130 CST Saturday and reopened at 0800 CST Monday. About 1,000 commercial trucks were expected to cross the border on Monday, Boyda said.

Winnipeg police said one man suffered a heart attack after shovelling snow. The Winnipeg Sun quoted ambulance attendants who said three deaths happened from either shovelling snow or pushing cars out of snow drifts.
"Flights this morning only left with slight delays because of all the people being rebooked after they were stranded here on Sunday," Winnipeg International Airport manager Colleen Rogers said.
Hundreds of passengers were stranded at Winnipeg's 24-hour airport after Air Canada, Canadian Airlines International and Northwest Airlines Corp decided not to fly out, she said.
"We have some delays but its not stopping our trains. Trains are backed up at Winnipeg's Symington (rail triage) yard," Canadian National Railway Co spokesman Scott Roberts said.
CP Rail System officials were not available for comment.

"Any train delays will be localized to southern Manitoba but nothing was shut down. Grain elevators do have snow drifts around them and it's bound to slow things up a bit but we don't perceive any major problems," Canadian Wheat Board spokeswoman Deanna Allen said.
Electric service from provincially-owned Manitoba Hydro was knocked down in rural areas, a company spokesman said.

The storm dumped 25 cm (10 inches) in the Red River Valley and 35 cm (14 inches) in Kenora, Ontario, and 40 cm (16 inches) at Red Lake, Ontario, Environment Canada meteorologist Clarence Spelchak said.
